sse_decoder.How does a chat completion API stream to: Over one HTTP response with text/event-stream: lines like "data: {json}" followed by a blank line, one event per chunk of tokens.
sse_decoder.Why can't a client decode each network c: The network cuts bytes anywhere: through a multi-byte character, or between \r and \n.
sse_decoder.Walk through what state the decoder keep: The bytes of the unfinished line, a pending carriage-return flag, and the fields of the unfinished event. A forgotten CR makes CRLF read as a line end plus an empty line, which dispatches the event too early.
sse_decoder.Why does the last event id persist acros: The id identifies the resume point, and the client sends it as Last-Event-ID when reconnecting. The name and data belong to one event only.
sse_decoder.Why does the OpenAI protocol end with a: A closed connection could be a network failure. An explicit end marker lets the client tell a finished stream from a cut one.
sse_decoder.SSE versus WebSockets versus gRPC stream: SSE is simple and proxy-friendly but one-way, and WebSockets are bidirectional but harder to proxy. gRPC is typed and fast but less supported in browsers.
sse_decoder.Streaming one event per token versus bat: One event per token gives the lowest latency but more overhead. Batching reduces overhead but makes text appear in jumps.

chat_stream_accumulator.What does a streamed chat completion chu: Deltas: a bit of content, or a tool-call fragment with an index. The client merges them into a snapshot of the message.
chat_stream_accumulator.How are parallel tool calls streamed, an: Each fragment carries the index of its call. The first fragment has the id, type and name; later ones add argument text.
chat_stream_accumulator.Why must index and type be replaced rath: They identify a call rather than carry content, so they must be replaced. Concatenating type gives "functionfunction", and adding indexes turns 1 + 1 into 2, a corrupt index in the snapshot.
chat_stream_accumulator.One chunk contains two fragments for the: A naive copy stores both fragments as separate list entries. Merging by index combines them into one call.
chat_stream_accumulator.Why should a null content delta never ov: Servers send null content alongside tool deltas. Overwriting would erase the text already received.
chat_stream_accumulator.Generic recursive delta merging versus a: Generic merging handles new fields automatically but cannot catch malformed output. Typed merging is strict but needs updates for each API change.
chat_stream_accumulator.Parsing tool arguments incrementally whi: Incremental parsing lets you show or start work early but needs a partial-JSON parser. Waiting is simpler and always valid.

incremental_detokenize.Why can't a streaming server decode each: Tokenizers drop leading spaces when decoding a lone token, and a character can span several byte tokens.
incremental_detokenize.What is byte-fallback tokenization, and: Rare characters are split into byte tokens. A partial sequence decodes to the replacement character.
incremental_detokenize.Walk through prefix_offset and read_offs: Step 1 emits the text; step 2 decodes to something ending in the replacement character, so it returns "" and keeps the offsets. Step 3 completes the character and emits it.
incremental_detokenize.Why is the window seeded with the last f: The first generated token needs context for its leading space. Without the prompt it would be decoded at the start of a string.
incremental_detokenize.Why does the detokenizer compare lengths: Decoding can merge or drop characters, so the new text may not be longer than the prefix. Then there is nothing new to send yet.
incremental_detokenize.Window-based incremental decoding (vLLM): The window approach is exact and fast. Word buffering is simple but adds latency and needs special handling for CJK, which has no spaces.
incremental_detokenize.Detokenizing in the engine process versu: A separate process frees the engine from GIL contention and isolates crashes, at the cost of IPC.

stop_string_holdback.What are stop strings in an LLM API, and: Text sequences that end generation. A stop string can span several tokens or be part of one.
stop_string_holdback.Why must a streaming server hold back so: The end of the text may be the start of a stop string. Once sent, it cannot be taken back.
stop_string_holdback.Why is the hold-back exactly the longest: At most len - 1 characters of a stop string can be at the end without it being complete. Example: stop "abc" with 1 held char leaks "a" when "ab" arrives.
stop_string_holdback.Where does the search for a stop string: New text plus len(s) - 1 characters before it, since a stop string can start in old text and end in new text.
stop_string_holdback.Speculative decoding appends several tok: The one that completes earliest in the text. That matches appending the tokens one at a time.
stop_string_holdback.Stop strings checked on detokenized text: Token ids are cheap and exact but miss strings with multiple tokenizations. Text matching is exact on output but costs detokenization.
stop_string_holdback.Holding back text for stop strings versu: Holding back adds a little latency but guarantees correct output. Client trimming is fast but can show text that should not appear.

request_output_collector.In an async LLM server, what sits betwee: A per-request collector or queue. Calling the handler directly would block the engine loop on slow clients.
request_output_collector.What is backpressure, and what happens t: Slowing the producer to match the consumer. Without it, a slow client makes outputs pile up in memory.
request_output_collector.Why does the collector merge outputs ins: Merging keeps memory constant: a slow client gets the same text in bigger chunks.
request_output_collector.Delta mode appends and cumulative mode r: Delta mode: "a", "b", "c" become "abc". Cumulative mode: "a", "ab", "abc" become "abc" (the latest).
request_output_collector.Why must merging match completions by in: With n > 1 samples, each index is a separate completion. An error must reach the client even if outputs are pending.
request_output_collector.One-slot merging versus a bounded queue: One slot never blocks the engine and keeps memory bounded, while a bounded queue blocks the producer. An unbounded queue risks running out of memory.
request_output_collector.Detecting client disconnects and abortin: Aborting saves GPU work, while finishing may help caching or retries. Consider idempotency when the client reconnects.

attention_sink_cache.What is an attention sink, and why does: Models dump attention mass on the first tokens. Evicting them shifts that mass elsewhere and perplexity explodes.
attention_sink_cache.What problem does StreamingLLM solve, an: Endless generation at constant memory without quality collapse. It does not extend memory of evicted content.
attention_sink_cache.Walk through evict-for-space when the ca: Keep the first start_size tokens and the last recent_size - n tokens, so the n new tokens fit.
attention_sink_cache.Why does StreamingLLM give keys position: Positions stay within the trained range. Text positions grow without bound and have gaps, which is out of distribution for RoPE.
attention_sink_cache.Why must the cache store keys before RoP: Positions change after eviction, so keys must be rotated again. Every cached key is rotated every step.
attention_sink_cache.Attention sinks plus a recent window ver: Sinks and a window are simple and work with standard kernels, while H2O adapts to content but needs attention scores. A learned sink is built into training.
attention_sink_cache.Bounded-memory streaming versus retrieva: Bounded memory is cheap but forgets. Retrieval can recall evicted facts but adds latency and complexity.

sink_cache_rerotation.Why can a RoPE key rotated at one positi: RoPE is a rotation. Rotations compose by adding angles, so rotating by -shift moves the position back.
sink_cache_rerotation.What does a sink cache keep and what doe: The first num_sink_tokens tokens and the most recent tokens. It evicts the oldest non-sink tokens.
sink_cache_rerotation.Derive the correction: a key rotated at: Rotate by -shift * frequencies. Sinks do not move, so their rotation is already correct.
sink_cache_rerotation.Compare storing keys before RoPE and rot: StreamingLLM re-rotates every cached key every step. SinkCache rotates each key once, and corrects all kept keys only on eviction.
sink_cache_rerotation.Why does repeated re-rotation accumulate: Every rotation rounds. In half precision errors add up; compute the correction in fp32.
sink_cache_rerotation.Correcting rotated keys on eviction vers: Fused RoPE in the kernel avoids the correction step but needs custom kernels. Correction works with standard kernels.
sink_cache_rerotation.Shipping a cache strategy inside the mod: In the library it is maintained and discoverable but adds maintenance burden. As Hub code it is lighter but easier to miss or break.

h2o_kv_eviction.What is a heavy hitter in the KV cache,: A token that receives a lot of attention over many steps. Past attention predicts future importance.
h2o_kv_eviction.Why does H2O keep a recent window in add: New tokens have not had time to accumulate score. Local context also matters for fluency.
h2o_kv_eviction.Walk through one decoding step: how are: Sum the new queries' attention over queries. Add the old scores to the first L - n columns, which are the old tokens.
h2o_kv_eviction.Why choose heavy hitters per head rather: Heads attend to different things. Per-head selection gives a ragged layout that paged kernels do not handle directly.
h2o_kv_eviction.How do attention sinks relate to H2O's h: The first tokens usually become heavy hitters on their own. Sinks are a fixed special case.
h2o_kv_eviction.H2O's accumulated scores versus SnapKV's: H2O needs attention weights that FlashAttention does not output, and SnapKV scores once from a window. Sinks need nothing.
h2o_kv_eviction.Irreversible eviction versus offloading: Eviction is simple but permanent. Offloading keeps everything but adds transfer latency and complexity.

duplex_streaming_session.What is a full-duplex interaction model,: The model listens and speaks at the same time in 200ms slices. Pipelines wait for the turn to end and add latency at each stage.
duplex_streaming_session.Why would sending every 200 ms chunk as: Each chunk would re-prefill the whole history. The session keeps the history and KV on the server.
duplex_streaming_session.After a request with a 6-token sequence: The last sampled token never ran through the model, so it has no KV. The KV length is 6 + 3 - 1 = 8.
duplex_streaming_session.Why commit history only when a request f: An aborted chunk leaves partial state. Committing only on finish lets the next chunk start from the last consistent point.
duplex_streaming_session.Why does a streaming session allow only: Each chunk depends on the previous output, so concurrent requests would race on the same KV. The BOS token only belongs at the very start.
duplex_streaming_session.One interleaved sequence of micro-turns: One sequence is simple but grows fast. Separate streams (Moshi) model overlap directly but need a more complex architecture.
duplex_streaming_session.Sticky sessions that pin KV on one GPU v: Sticky sessions are fast but tie the user to one GPU. Stateless requests with prefix caching are flexible but pay cache misses.

embodied_action_stream.How does an agent like SIMA 2 turn a lan: The model outputs structured text that is parsed deterministically into keyboard and mouse events.
embodied_action_stream.Why do embodied agents emit actions in c: Inference is slower than the game's frame rate. Each chunk was computed from a frame that is already old when it runs.
embodied_action_stream.A new chunk arrives while the old plan s: Drop the old plan's future events, release every key still held (sorted), then schedule the new chunk's actions.
embodied_action_stream.Why should a malformed chunk be rejected: Half a plan is not what the model intended. Keeping the old plan running is the safer fallback.
embodied_action_stream.How does a slow planner issuing instruct: The planner sets goals slowly and the controller acts fast. A controller acting on stale instructions pursues outdated goals.
embodied_action_stream.Text actions from a general LLM versus a: Text actions are general but slower and less precise. A dedicated action head is fast and precise but narrow.
embodied_action_stream.Long action chunks versus short chunks w: Long chunks are smooth but react slowly. Short chunks react quickly but cost more inference.

posed_frame_context.How can a video model act as a world mod: It predicts the next frame from previous frames. The frames and their camera poses are the memory.
posed_frame_context.Why can't a real-time world model condit: Cost grows with every frame. Real time needs a bounded context.
posed_frame_context.Walk through choosing context for a came: Frames facing the opposite way show different content. Filter by direction first, then rank by distance.
posed_frame_context.Why always include the most recent frame: They carry motion and lighting continuity, which keeps the stream smooth.
posed_frame_context.How does pose-based retrieval make the w: Old frames of a place are retrieved again when you return, so it looks the same.
posed_frame_context.Retrieval by pose heuristics versus lear: Pose heuristics are cheap but miss occlusion, and learned retrieval adapts but costs more. Explicit 3D is consistent but less general.
posed_frame_context.Spending the real-time frame budget on m: More context improves consistency and more steps improve quality. Both cost latency.
